claims.text: The baseline Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy is a single-phase BCC material.
Asymmetric XRD peaks in the baseline alloy indicate dendritic-versus-interdendritic compositional micro-segregation.
The baseline alloy has significantly reduced room-temperature fracture strain.
Approximately 4 at.% Cr is added to the Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy.
Annealing below the Laves-phase solvus will allow Cr to partition into interdendritic regions without completely dissolving the Laves phase.
Cr addition drives formation of a Cr-rich, multicomponent Laves phase.
The Cr-containing secondary phase has a volume fraction of approximately 4%.
The Laves phase is likely C14 or C15 type.
The Laves phase forms a reticulated or interconnected network at grain boundaries or interdendritic regions.
The reticulated Laves phase impedes propagating cracks by causing crack deflection, branching, or bridging.
Crack deflection, branching, and bridging increase fracture-surface area and energy dissipation, thereby toughening the alloy.
Substitution of larger Hf or Zr atoms by smaller Cr atoms contracts the BCC lattice and shifts XRD peaks to higher 2θ.
Cr-induced lattice contraction increases lattice distortion and the friction stress for dislocation motion, producing solid-solution hardening.
The combined secondary-phase and solid-solution effects increase room-temperature fracture strain relative to the Cr-free baseline.
The combined effects restore fracture strain to theoretical expectations.
The low baseline fracture strain results from brittle crack propagation along segregation boundaries.
Cr contents above approximately 4 at.% may generate an excessive fraction of brittle Laves phase and reduce ductility.
More than 11 vol.% Laves phase caused low plasticity in CrMoNbWV alloys.
The hypothesis requires a measurable contraction of the BCC lattice, operationally indicated by an XRD peak shift to higher 2θ.
Laves-phase morphology is sensitive to local composition and cooling rate.
